data.title: ComEd Debuts Mobile Assistance Unit at Waukegan Resource Fair, Bringing On-Site Bill Help Directly to Customers
data.description:
ComEd Debuts Mobile Assistance Unit at Waukegan Resource Fair, Bringing On-Site Bill Help Directly to Customers

Fleet of mobile office vehicles are ComEd’s latest effort to expand bill-assistance and energy-saving programs and bring them directly into northern Illinois communities

TodayComEd unveiled the first of its new Mobile Assistance Unit activations during Waukegan Township's Corner of Hope & Opportunity Community Resource Fair & Block Party. The appearance marked the debut of a fleet of vehicles equipped to deliver bill-assistance services anywhere across ComEd's northern Illinois service territory.

Waukegan Township's Resource Fair and Block Party, held annually since 2024, brings together health services, child and adult programs, job-training opportunities and other community resources in one place. ComEd has taken part in community resource fairs since 2025 in collaboration with local organizations to help meet customers where they are with support.

"Getting help should be simple, and it should be close to home," said Ajit Apte, senior vice president of Customer Operations, ComEd. "Our new Mobile Assistance Units allow us to bring meaningful, in-person support directly to the neighborhoods we serve, connecting customers with the programs and tools that can help manage their energy bills."

The event is one of nearly a dozen community resource fairs ComEd plans to take part in during 2026 as part of a growing effort to expand bill-support services and bring them directly to customers. This is critical as energy supply prices continue to rise due to energy demand outpacing the rate of new supply options coming online. ComEd does not set these prices and does not profit from them. On site, ComEd representatives helped customers access bill-assistance programs, enroll in new affordability offerings and explore energy-saving tools.

"Waukegan Township and our partners here on the corner of Hope and Opportunity are proud to once again welcome ComEd to our third annual Community Resource Fair & Block Party," said Marc Jones, Waukegan Township Supervisor. "This year's event is especially exciting with the presence of a ComEd Mobile Assistance Unit, creating another convenient way for customers to access energy support. By bringing these services directly to community events, we can help more residents connect with resources that benefit their daily lives."

The Mobile Assistance Units are part of ComEd's fleet of storm-response vehicles, repurposed to support customers with bill assistance during periods when they are not actively deployed for power restoration. These vehicles normally play an essential role supporting area teams during storms and large-scale restoration events, serving as field-based hubs equipped with connectivity, power generation and workspace. By putting these vehicles to work in the community during fair weather days, ComEd can bring personalized bill support, payment options, assistance-program enrollment and energy-efficiency education directly into neighborhoods and community gathering spaces.

"Families and businesses across our community continue to face challenges as the cost of everyday necessities remains high. That's why it's so important to create opportunities where residents can connect with multiple forms of support in one place," said Waukegan Mayor Sam Cunningham. "Events like this help ensure people are aware of available resources, from utility bill assistance to financial and community services, while making it easier to get questions answered and access help when they need it most."

At the Waukegan fair, ComEd offered enrollment support for a range of programs created to help customers navigate rising costs, including:

  • The Low-Income Discount (LID) program, launched in January 2026, provides qualifying income-eligible customers a percentage-based discount on their monthly electric bill based on income level.
  • ComEd's new Time-of-Day Pricing rate, launched this summer, which helps households save money by shifting energy use to times when electricity prices are lower and demand is reduced.
  • ComEd's bill-assistance and bill-management options, including Budget Billing, payment arrangements and High Usage Alerts, which can help customers better manage monthly energy costs and avoid unexpected bill increases
  • The ComEd Energy Efficiency Program, which offers tools, incentives and resources to help residential and business customers reduce energy use and lower costs.

These efforts reflect ComEd's commitment to The Exelon Promise, a customer-focused strategy from ComEd's parent company, Exelon, aimed at providing quick relief, strong protections and lasting solutions to rising energy costs.

Customers can find more information about ComEd's bill-assistance options and check their eligibility through ComEd’s Smart Assistance Manager (SAM) at ComEd.com/SAM.

ComEd is a unit of Chicago-based Exelon Corporation (NASDAQ: EXC), a Fortune 200 company and one of the nation’s largest utility companies, serving more than 10.7 million electricity and natural gas customers. ComEd powers the lives of more than 4.2 million customers across northern Illinois, or 70 percent of the state’s population. For more information, visit ComEd.com, and connect with the company on Facebook, Instagram, LinkedIn, X and YouTube.

ComEd

data.description:
There are positive (a monthly income) and maybe not-so-positive (writing letters to future grandchildren to be opened upon your death) ways of making sure that your legacy remains. An annuity is a fine idea, but set it up and let it go (until your next estate review).

You mention that you would not fully have faith in your daughter handling a large sum of money and/or believe there's a risk she could be subject to undue influence from a friend or partner, if she did have a lot of money sitting in her bank account.

That tells me that, perhaps, she has some self-reflection to do. And, sometimes, when people feel unhappy or resentful, rather than look at their own choices, they look for people to blame. I'm sorry that you appear to be that person in this situation.

data.title: 'The estrangement isn't about politics': My daughter hasn't spoken to me for 4 years. Do I leave her a monthly annuity?
data.description:
By Quentin Fottrell

'You'll have to trust me when I tell you that she had love, support and opportunities'

"I also believe parents shouldn't give their estranged children the power to negatively control their emotions or lives." (Photo subject is a model.)

Dear Quentin,

I'm the guy who wrote to you - and was published - who is 70, still working, loving it, and taking a week off every month ("After 46 years working, I'm not retiring - instead, I take a vacation every month. Is that a good life in your 70s?").

I really appreciate your thoughtful, considered opinions. Your recent letter about the estranged son and daughter-in-law hit home for me ("Our son and daughter-in-law cut us out of their lives after a political argument. Should we change our $3 million will?").

I have four kids - two are mine and two are my wife's - but they are all ours in every meaningful sense. My daughter hasn't spoken to me in four years. She occasionally communicates through Facebook with my previous spouse, with whom I'm still close.

The estrangement isn't about politics. She blames us - and her biological brother - for everything bad that happened to her. You'll have to trust me when I tell you that she had love, support and opportunities above and beyond what most kids receive.

If we ever reconcile, the estate plan can always be changed.

I'm currently rewriting my estate plan. I previously wrote my daughter out of it, but I review my estate plan every couple of years because life changes every couple of years. The letter writer described her decision as irreversible. It isn't irreversible until we die.

We've decided to provide my daughter with a monthly life annuity. She has no children, and the amount will be less than what the others will receive directly. The income will protect the money from her and, potentially, from people around her who might take advantage of her.

If she had children, I would consider structuring the trust to help with things like education or a first home. I'd also make sure there was a corporate trustee or a truly trusted friend involved, because I wouldn't trust my daughter to manage a large inheritance herself.

In my case, the monthly annuity for my estranged daughter will be a reminder, every month for the rest of her life, that her father was still there and still cared about her. If we ever reconcile, the estate plan can always be changed.

Don't miss: I don't want to leave my financially irresponsible daughter my house. Is that unreasonable?

The emotional side

On the emotional side, I believe time can change things. I never give up hope because a father - or mother - always hopes for a better outcome for their children. But I also believe parents shouldn't give their estranged children the power to negatively control their emotions or lives.

At some point, I think the parents have to give the kids exactly what they say they want: total estrangement. Stop trying. Stop sending the messages. Stop chasing them. Let them go. That is incredibly hard, especially when grandchildren are involved.

It's truly a tragedy when families become casualties of things that, in the long run, may not matter nearly as much as the people involved. If my daughter had children and refused to let me see them, I'd handwrite a letter to each grandchild every birthday and/or holiday.

I'd tell them how much I missed them and describe the things we would be doing together if I were allowed to be part of their lives. Most importantly, I'd tell them that I loved them. Then I'd seal and date every letter and put them away.

Stop trying. Stop sending the messages. Stop chasing them.

Maybe someday I'd have the opportunity to give those letters to my grandchildren when they were old enough to understand why they had an absent grandfather. There's a risk they could end up being read at my graveside. So be it.

There's also a risk that doing this could eventually damage my daughter's relationship with her own children. But, honestly, I don't think that would change my decision. The grandchildren deserve to know that they were loved, even if that love had to exist in absentia.

I think that could mean a great deal to them someday. So my advice to the parents who wrote you that letter about falling out with their son and daughter-in-law would be: Give the estranged children what they say they want and leave them alone - truly alone.

And, of course, politics is temporary. Republicans and Democrats will come and go. Time and reality have a way of changing people's perspectives, and I suspect many people will eventually regret some of the choices they made while they were angry.

Father & Husband

Related: 'This is a tricky subject': We're in our 70s and our only child is 40. Do we leave her everything?

You can email The Moneyist with any financial and ethical questions at qfottrell@marketwatch.com. The Moneyist regrets he cannot reply to questions individually.

Sometimes, the hardest thing to do is to love someone from afar, and support them from afar.

Dear Father,

Thank you for sharing your story.

People do share in great detail here all the time, but yours is deeply personal. I appreciate that your goal is to help others, and assure parents who are going through something similar that it does, indeed, get better. After four years, you are clearly still adjusting to this new normal.

Letting go is a decision, but it's often a daily practice too, as you have no doubt discovered. What struck me about the father and mother whose son and daughter-in-law cut off contact due to their differences over politics and religion was the finality in his letter.

You are walking a line, knowing that you cannot keep trying to control what someone else does or doesn't do, but also not allowing an experience of loss and frustration to control you. It's not as easy as it seems, especially for someone you love, and I applaud you for that.

Letting go is a decision, a hard one, but it's often also a daily practice.

Sometimes, the hardest thing to do is to love someone from afar, and support them from afar, and quell those feelings of anger and/or confusion that may come up from time to time. Allowing someone space and time is a gift, and it's probably the most selfless kind of gift.

About those letters. Your instinct is right: Express your love for any future grandchildren in writing, but also know that leaving a stash of letters behind could also damage their relationship with their mother and, even if it wasn't your intention, serve as a kind of payback for cutting ties.

Reading between the lines, I feel like you are unsure about putting any grandchildren in the position of having to decipher the past and/or take sides in an adult conflict, especially before they are old enough to do so. "I love you" says everything they need to know.

The letters form a bridge, one that may not allow you to let go completely and free yourself from the more difficult aspects of this estrangement. Setting up a trust and/or bequest is a way you can take action; that can do far more than words, which are open to misinterpretation, can.

Don't miss: Can I claim 50% of my husband's Social Security now - and switch to my higher benefit at 70?

Financial plan

One of the trickiest parts about having an estranged child is dealing with estate planning. Like I said to the previous letter writer, there's no right or wrong way to go about that. Some people write to me and say, "I'll cut them out of my life in every way." And that's their decision.

Others, like you, make plans to provide their estranged child with an income, even a modest one, or make provisions for their grandchildren through a trust or 529 plan. That's generous and it takes not a small amount of magnanimity to put aside hurt feelings like that.

Marital trusts are extremely useful for blended families, so each spouse ensures that their respective children are taken care of if one of them dies. A special-needs trust or spendthrift trust can also distribute funds based on need, including medical bills.

If one child or grandchild decides to go to college, the trust can provide for that. If another child falls off the wagon and needs rehab, the trust could fund that too. The tax benefits help to ensure that a significantly higher portion of your estate passes to your children tax-free.

Sometimes when people feel unhappy, they look for someone to blame.

An irrevocable trust can move assets and their future growth out of your taxable estate. But putting money into a trust is treated as a taxable gift, though many people can offset that using the annual exclusion or their lifetime gift exemption ($15 million or $30 million for a married couple).

For example, a third-party special-needs trust allows you to support a disabled adult child without jeopardizing their eligibility for government benefits, primarily because the assets never legally belong to them. And spendthrift protections can help shield trust assets from creditors.

Depending on how a trust is set up, income can be taxed to the trust itself, the beneficiary or the grantor. The biggest tax advantages usually come from using an irrevocable trust to move future appreciation outside your estate while still keeping strong asset-protection features in place.

The real value of trusts often lies in asset protection, long-term stability, and preserving access to government benefits. As you point out, there's the emotional side. Sometimes we create these structures because they give us a sense of order when all else feels out of our control.

Income can be taxed to the trust itself, the beneficiary, or the grantor. That's you.

data.title: 'We are committed Christians': Our son and daughter-in-law cut us off over politics. Should we change our $3 million will?
data.description:
By Quentin Fottrell

'We are hurt and confused, but we have also tried to respect the boundaries they have established'

"We don't want political or religious differences to permanently destroy our relationship." (Photo subjects are models.)

Dear Quentin,

My wife and I are in our early 70s and in good health. Our net worth is $3 million and could eventually grow to more than $4 million because of an anticipated inheritance from an aging family member. We have two sons, both in their late 30s. Our estate plan currently includes a trust and wills that divide our assets equally between them after we are both gone.

One of our sons recently got married. For many years, we have tried to preserve family unity by agreeing as a family not to discuss politics, because we knew those conversations could become divisive. Recently, however, political issues came up, and our daughter-in-law wanted to discuss and debate them with me. I calmly reminded them of our previous agreement.

Since January, our son and his wife have stopped communicating with my wife and me. They have refused to return our phone calls or respond to our texts. We have been told that our daughter-in-law does not wish to have contact with our family. Some very painful things were said, primarily by our daughter-in-law, as we made a conscious effort not to respond in kind.

Our political views and Christian faith were criticized. We are conservative politically and committed Christians, while they hold very different beliefs. What has been especially difficult is that we don't really know exactly what was said or done that resulted in what appears to be a complete cutoff in communication. They have not responded to our attempts to reach out.

We are hurt and confused, but we have also tried to respect the boundaries they have established. At the same time, we love our son deeply. We don't want political or religious differences to permanently destroy our relationship with him, and we want to leave the door open for reconciliation without creating additional conflict or pressure.

We are also wrestling with a difficult question about our estate plan. Given the current circumstances, we have considered whether we should remove this son from our will or otherwise change the way his inheritance would be handled. We do not want our hard-earned assets to ultimately benefit someone with whom we currently have such a difficult relationship.

We recognize that making a decision about an inheritance while we are hurt could be a mistake. We plan to consult an estate-planning attorney and want to approach this thoughtfully rather than making an irreversible decision out of anger or emotion. Our greatest hope is that, somehow, there will eventually be a path back to a relationship with our son and his family.

What do your readers think? What should we do?

Father and Husband

Related: 'This is a tricky subject': We're in our 70s and our only child is 40. Do we leave her everything?

You can email The Moneyist with any financial and ethical questions at qfottrell@marketwatch.com. The Moneyist regrets he cannot reply to questions individually.

We often take our politics and religion, whether we are on the right or left of the spectrum, very personally.

Dear Father,

I can't tell you to disinherit your son and daughter-in-law, and I can't tell you not to do so.

It's a very personal decision, and one that will inevitably evolve with time. If they eventually have children, you may wish to leave money in a trust for your grandchildren - a tax-advantaged 529 account for college or an income or lump sum when they turn 21 or 30 - or you may decide that you have become so estranged that it's too late to leave your money to people who want nothing to do with you.

There is no right or wrong answer, whether you are a Christian conservative or an agnostic liberal (or a Christian liberal or agnostic conservative). What is more certain is that we often take our politics and religion, whether we are on the right or left of the spectrum, in a deeply personal way, particularly in a country so polarized. Society's beliefs are reflected in our choices, lifestyles and, yes, political policies.

Ultimately, it will come down to the amount of time that passes and the depth of the fissure between you and your son and daughter-in-law. It's still early days, and it hurts. Time might act as a salve, making it easier for you to divide your estate 50/50 between your sons, or it might solidify your belief that your money should go to a child who wants to maintain a relationship.

The problem with seeking the advice of others is that they will give you an opinion colored by their own experience.

There are, for better or for worse, some clear reasons to either cut a child out of your will or leave them an income with strict conditions in a special-needs trust. Those reasons include financial recklessness, substance-misuse issues, gambling problems or simply because you don't want an in-law to get their hands on your life savings. Again, no judgment.

Andreea Nica, an associate professor of sociology at Western New Mexico University in Silver Lake, N.M., recently published a study in Frontiers in Sociology, a peer-reviewed journal, in which she concluded that estrangement between adult children and parents has become increasingly common in recent years, but the end result can sometimes be a positive one.

Nica conducted 30 online interviews about how children and parents experience estrangement. Interviewees told her that their respective estrangements were not necessarily good or bad. Many participants built new support networks through friends, partners, therapy, spirituality and support groups. Hard as it may seem now to comprehend, some people developed healthier relationships with others and had a stronger sense of their own place in the world.

Don't miss: I found a $100 bill in the communal washer at my Airbnb. What should I do?

The Greek chorus

You ask what other people think. The problem with seeking the advice of others - whether they are readers of an advice column or your own friends, relatives and neighbors - is that they will give you an opinion that is colored by their own experience. Are they estranged from their parents or children? Are they conservative, like you, or liberal, like your son and daughter-in-law? That all influences their take.

One member of the Moneyist Facebook Group would draw a line in the sand. "I wouldn't leave one son out of your will simply because his political views differ from yours," she writes. "My husband and I are on the opposite end of the political spectrum - we're fairly middle-of-the-road liberals, while our son is a strong Trump supporter.

"I generally avoid discussing politics with him," she continues. "My husband sometimes forgets and brings it up. One time, our son became quite upset with his father. He later called to apologize, and I told him it was OK. At the end of the day, we live in America, and we're allowed to have very different political views - even when we think the other person is wrong."

Estrangement is painful, confusing and frustrating, and it also comes with some real-world consequences.

Another reader suggests making another attempt at communication: "Reach out to your son directly and ask him what, specifically, was said or done that offended or hurt them - yes, them, not just your daughter-in-law. If there is something you can understand, acknowledge and negotiate, that's a place to start rebuilding the relationship.

"If the conflict ultimately comes down to political or religious beliefs, you're certainly not alone," she adds. "But perhaps this could be an opportunity for some self-reflection. Consider asking yourself why your beliefs might have led someone who loves you deeply to distance themselves from you. If you do that, I'd encourage you to step outside your usual echo chamber."

You are going through something that, unfortunately, many families have experienced. It's painful, confusing and frustrating, and it comes with some real-world consequences: access to grandchildren, peace of mind (at least for a time), inheritance issues and, yes, the opportunity to navigate the world without having to walk on eggshells or suppress your feelings and opinions.

Take your time before making a decision about your estate planning, and review your decision every year.

data.title: Canada announces retaliatory tariffs on U.S. goods after trade talks break down
data.description:
By Rey Mashayekhi

Canadian Prime Minister Mark Carney speaks at a press conference in Ottawa, Ontario, on Saturday after trade talks with the U.S. collapsed.

Canada Prime Minister Mark Carney on Saturday announced his country would impose "dollar-for-dollar" tariffs on U.S. goods - a retaliatory measure after trade talks between the two nations broke down late Friday, leading the U.S. to levy 50% tariffs on roughly $20 billion in Canadian goods.

Carney said the tariffs would take effect next month on the Tuesday after Labor Day, and would focus on sectors including steel, dairy, paper, electronics, appliances and agricultural equipment.

"While we believed earlier this week that we were moving toward a mutually beneficial agreement, in recent days, the U.S. proposed new terms that were uneconomic, unfair and undermined the net benefits to Canada, calling into question the reliability of any deal," Carney said at a press conference in Ottawa.

"In short, they asked too much and offered too little," the prime minister added.

The two sides entered trade negotiations after President Donald Trump announced 50% tariffs on Canadian goods last month - the latest in a series of trade disputes between the North American neighbors since Trump returned to the White House last year. The U.S. president has taken a similar stance against American trade partners globally.

After promising that the duties would go into effect on Wednesday, Trump back down on that threat late Tuesday, saying that the U.S. and Canada were close to a deal. Yet talks collapsed on Friday evening, and the U.S.'s 50% tariffs on Canadian imports came into effect shortly after midnight Saturday.

Carney said Saturday that his government had made the decision to impose tariffs of its own "reluctantly, because we recognize that it will raise costs and reduce choice for Canadians." He said Canada had been willing to drop existing retaliatory tariffs on "strategic sectors" like steel, aluminum and automobiles if the U.S. "substantially lowered theirs," and would have encouraged its provinces to return American alcohol to store shelves.

But the prime minister said Canada was "not prepared to compromise" its sovereignty nor its "protection of the French language and our culture" in the negotiations. He added that the new tariffs are "a focused response to protect and defend our industries and allow them to compete with U.S. products in the Canadian market."

Representatives for the White House could not immediately be reached for comment.

-Rey Mashayekhi

data.title: 'She looked into COBRA': My friend was laid off and lost her health insurance. How can she find affordable coverage?
data.description:
By Quentin Fottrell

'The cost is absolutely ridiculous'

"Would she qualify for an ACA Marketplace plan through a special enrollment period?" (Photo subject is a model.)

Dear Quentin,

My friend in Wisconsin was laid off and was told that her health insurance through her employer ends at midnight. She looked into COBRA, but the cost is absolutely ridiculous.

Do you have suggestions for affordable health-insurance options she could look into? Would she qualify for an Affordable Care Act Marketplace plan through a special enrollment period because she lost her job and employer-sponsored coverage?

Also, could enrolling in college courses make her eligible for a student health-insurance plan that would be more affordable?

She's desperate to find coverage.

Trying to Help

Don't miss: 'Too many people go bankrupt': Should Medicare provide catastrophic coverage?

You can email The Moneyist with any financial and ethical questions at qfottrell@marketwatch.com. The Moneyist regrets he cannot reply to questions individually.

With the ACA Marketplace, she has a 60-day window after the loss of her coverage to pick a plan.

Dear Trying,

The ACA Marketplace or a state healthcare plan are the best options for your friend.

She is correct: Losing workplace health insurance qualifies your friend, or anyone else in a similar position, for a special enrollment period on HealthCare.gov. She has a 60-day window after the loss of her coverage to pick a plan. The ACA Marketplace may ask for documents, including an employer or insurer notice, to verify when her coverage came to an end.

The ACA Marketplace calculates her premium based on her age, location, household size and expected household income for the entire calendar year, not necessarily her own individual income. The most important takeaway at this juncture is that she can apply outside the normal open-enrollment period, given that she lost her job.

She may also qualify for an ACA subsidy. If she was earning, say, $45,000 before being laid off and, assuming she doesn't have another job to go to, will earn significantly less for the remainder of the year, she will have to estimate her total income for 2026, which includes her salary up until the time she was laid off and unemployment benefits.

Universities offer student health plans, but premiums can range roughly from $1,500 to $3,000 or more for the academic year, and that doesn't include tuition. Nor are they eligible for federal ACA Marketplace subsidies. Most students save more by staying on their parents' health plan until 26, if eligible, or look into Medicaid or the ACA Marketplace, which brings your friend full circle.

Don't miss: 'There is considerable tension': My grandmother, 99, wants to cut my mother out of her will. Should I intervene?

Sticker shock

Don't assume the ACA Marketplace will always be cheaper. She can apply for BadgerCare Plus through the ACCESS Wisconsin portal. BadgerCare Plus eligibility is based on current income, so this sounds like a good possibility for her. What's more, there is no asset test for most adults under 65 who qualify through the rules based on their modified adjusted gross income (MAGI).

MAGI is calculated using your adjusted gross income, taking certain adjustments or deductions into account. It's used to determine eligibility for certain tax deductions and credits, as well as certain government benefits and surcharges, according to Fidelity. The formula can also change depending on what benefits the individual is applying for.

If she applies through the ACA Marketplace and her income appears low enough for Medicaid rather than Marketplace subsidies, the application should likely be referred to the relevant state program. Given that she has just lost her job and her income has dropped substantially, tell her to check both BadgerCare Plus and ACA Marketplace plans before committing to COBRA.

People often get sticker shock when they investigate COBRA. As an individual, you are required to pay the full cost of your health-insurance plan, rather than just the portion that was deducted from your paycheck. You may actually be charged up to 102% of the premium - the amount your employer previously paid, in addition to your share of the premium and a 2% administrative fee.

COBRA can cost several hundred dollars a month for an individual, and family coverage can cost $1,500 or more per month, depending on the plan. Again, she likely has 60 days to elect COBRA, and once she pays the required premiums, her coverage can be applied retroactively to when her employer coverage ended.

To qualify for COBRA, the U.S. Labor Department says she must have been covered by her employer's group health plan, the plan must be subject to COBRA, and she must experience a qualifying event that causes her to lose coverage. For most private employers, federal COBRA applies to plans maintained by employers with 20 or more employees.

The takeaway: Enrolling as a student or taking out COBRA are not the only options.

data.title: FIA Celebrates Over Ninety Years of Supporting Motor Sport in the United States at the INDYCAR Freedom 250 Grand Prix of Washington D.C.
data.description:
FIA Celebrates Over Ninety Years of Supporting Motor Sport in the United States at the INDYCAR Freedom 250 Grand Prix of Washington D.C.

  • The FIA has been a part of American motor sport for almost a century since officiating land speed record attempts in the U.S. during the 1930s
  • The Freedom 250 Grand Prix is underpinned by over a decade of collaboration between the FIA and INDYCAR
  • World-leading FIA safety standards continue to protect drivers across the United States

The Fédération Internationale de l'Automobile (FIA), the global governing body for motor sport and the federation for mobility organisations worldwide, is celebrating almost a century of motor sport history and legacy in the United States ahead of the highly anticipated Freedom 250 NTT INDYCAR SERIES race this weekend marking 250 years of American independence.

This press release features multimedia. View the full release here: https://www.businesswire.com/news/home/20260822064940/en/

Motor sport safety has always been a central mission of the FIA and this weekend every driver lining up on the NTT INDYCAR SERIES grid will use FIA-approved driver safety equipment including helmets manufactured to FIA international standards, shaped by the Federation's decades of safety research across disciplines from Formula 1 to rallying, and rigorously validated through crash testing before ever reaching the grid.

The FIA’s connection with American motor sport dates back to the 1930s when the Federation officiated land speed records on the iconic salt flats of Bonneville, Utah. A couple of decades later the 1950 Indianapolis 500 would count as a round of the inaugural Formula One World Championship calendar, linking one of America’s most historic races with the pinnacle of international motor sport.

Over the decades that followed, the United States Grand Prix travelled across the nation with each venue helping to introduce new generations of fans to world-class competition while the invention of karting in California in August 1956, paved the way for greater participation in motor sport based on karts originally built steel tubes and a lawnmower engine.

Under the leadership of FIA President H.E. Mohammed Ben Sulayem, the United States now hosts a record number of FIA world championship rounds with races for the FIA Formula One World Championship, ABB FIA Formula E World Championship and FIA World Endurance Championship.

This year the United States will host five FIA World Championship rounds including three iconic circuits for the FIA Formula One World Championship calendar at the Miami Grand Prix, the United States Grand Prix in Texas and the Las Vegas Grand Prix. The Miami e-Prix featured on the 2026 ABB FIA Formula E World Championship calendar, and the upcoming six-hour Lone Star Le Mans race forms part of the 2026 FIA World Endurance Championship calendar.

In partnership with the FIA Member Club, the Automobile Competition Committee for the United States (ACCUS), motor sport in the United States is set to grow even further over the coming months and years. A successful candidate event staged earlier this year has laid the path for a return of the FIA World Rally Championship to the United States from next year, whilst Karting is set to celebrate 70 years of history later this year following its invention in California in August 1956.

Additionally, history was made earlier this month as the FIA confirmed a new provisional World Land Speed Record for a hydrogen internal combustion-powered vehicle, as the JCB Hydromax recorded a speed of 406.320 miles per hour / 653.909 kilometres per hour on the Bonneville Salt Flats in Utah, USA.

H.E. Mohammed Ben Sulayem, President of the FIA, said: “The FIA has played a key role in American motorsport for almost a century and we are proud to see the Freedom 250 NTT INDYCAR SERIES race pairing 250 years of American achievement with a sport that embodies speed, ingenuity and the freedom of the open road. The United States has played an important role in the history and the continued growth of global motorsport and today that contribution is stronger than ever, with a growing fanbase, a world-leading automotive industry, and some of the most exciting races in the world.

“This is a landmark event, and it is an honour for the FIA to be a part of it. Congratulations to President Trump, the U.S. Government, INDYCAR, our Member Club ACCUS, and all involved on making this vision a reality.”

The Fédération Internationale de l'Automobile (FIA) is the governing body for world motor sport and the federation for mobility organisations globally. It is a non-profit organisation committed to driving innovation and championing safety, sustainability and equality across motor sport and mobility.

Founded in 1904, with offices in Paris, London and Geneva, the FIA brings together 245 Member Organisations across five continents, representing millions of road users, motor sport professionals and volunteers. It develops and enforces regulations for motor sport, including six FIA World Championships, to ensure worldwide competitions are safe and fair for all.

For media enquiries, please contact:
Omar Sharif, Sport Communications Manager: osharif@fia.com

data.title: The Apex Institute Reveals What Hiring Managers Actually Want in Cloud and AI Infrastructure Roles
data.description:
The Apex Institute Reveals What Hiring Managers Actually Want in Cloud and AI Infrastructure Roles

The Apex Institute Reveals What Hiring Managers Actually Want in Cloud and AI Infrastructure Roles

PR Newswire

BOWIE, Md., Aug. 22, 2026

Job seekers spend most of their energy guessing what employers want. The people actually doing the hiring say the answer is simpler than most candidates think.

BOWIE, Md., Aug. 22, 2026 /PRNewswire/ -- Hiring managers filling cloud and AI infrastructure roles decide on four things: whether they trust you with a system that costs money when it breaks, whether you can explain a technical problem in plain language, whether you can point to real work you did, and how you behave when you do not know an answer. Skill only gets you past the first filter.

Most career advice is written from one side of the table. How to write a resume, how to answer interview questions, how to follow up. Almost none of it comes from the people actually deciding who gets hired.

That is the more useful conversation, says Tayo Lusi, founder of The Apex Institute. His training program tracks hiring patterns across cloud and infrastructure roles closely, and he says most candidates optimize for the wrong thing.

"Job seekers think hiring managers are looking for the smartest person in the room," Tayo said. "Most of the time, they are looking for the person they trust the least to cause a problem at two in the morning."

What do hiring managers actually decide on?

Four things, in roughly this order.

  1. Trust. Would they hand you a system that costs real money and real downtime if it breaks.
  2. Communication. Can you explain a technical problem to someone who is not technical.
  3. Proof of real work. Can you point at something you built and say what problem it solved.
  4. Handling uncertainty. What you do when you hit something you do not know.

Does the most technically skilled candidate win?

Rarely. Skill is the entry fee, not the deciding factor.

Technical skill gets you through the first filter. It proves you can do the work at a baseline. Past that point the skill gap between finalists shrinks, and something else decides it.

That something else is trust. Hiring managers are not only asking whether you can build something. They are asking whether they want you paged at midnight when it goes down. If you want to know what to learn and in what order before any of this matters, the free Cloud Engineering Career Path Roadmap lays out the sequence.

Why does clear communication matter so much?

Because cloud and AI infrastructure roles are never isolated. You explain technical problems to non technical people, write documentation other engineers rely on, and stay calm describing what went wrong during an outage.

Candidates who can only speak in technical language raise a quiet red flag. Hiring managers read it as risk. If you cannot explain a problem clearly in an interview, they wonder how you will explain a production issue at 3 a.m. to a team already under pressure.

What counts as proof of real work?

A resume full of tool names says almost nothing. Everyone lists the same platforms and certifications. What separates candidates is pointing at something they built and explaining the problem it solved.

"A project with a clear before and after is worth more than five certifications," Tayo said. "I have sat across from candidates who could not explain why the thing they built mattered. That is a bigger problem than not knowing enough tools."

This is the common blind spot for graduates of traditional coding and IT programs. They finish with a list of completed lessons and no story about impact. Hiring managers notice that gap immediately.

Get the free Cloud Project Portfolio Blueprint and build the one project a hiring manager will actually ask about.

How should you handle not knowing an answer?

Say so, then explain how you would find out. That answer beats a confident guess almost every time.

Nobody walks in knowing a company's specific systems, and hiring managers expect gaps. They are watching how you respond when you hit one. Someone who guesses confidently and gets it wrong is a bigger risk than someone honest about the gap, because in infrastructure work false confidence under pressure does more damage than missing knowledge.

Why are cloud and AI infrastructure roles harder to fill right now?

Because spending on this area is rising while hiring slows elsewhere. Roles sit open longer here than almost any other category in tech. The U.S. Bureau of Labor Statistics projects continued growth across computer and information technology occupations through the decade, with demand concentrated near infrastructure and security.

That pressure does not lower the bar on trust and communication. It raises it, because a bad infrastructure hire is more expensive to unwind than almost any other role. And when you do reach the offer, the free Tech Salary Negotiation Scripts and the free Cloud Engineering Salary Benchmark cover what the role is worth and how to ask for it.

Can these qualities be taught?

That is the bet The Apex Institute is built on. Most programs teach the technical skill and leave the rest to the candidate. Here, communication, documented proof of work and how you handle uncertainty are part of the curriculum rather than an afterthought.

Students have reported more than $11 million in combined job offers across 41 people. Individual results vary and are not typical.

"We are not just trying to teach people cloud infrastructure," Tayo said. "We are trying to teach people to think like the person on the other side of the interview table, because that is who decides whether they get hired."

The longer term goal is bigger than any one cohort. The company aims to impact millions of lives globally, including future nonprofit initiatives in developing countries teaching foundational cloud and tech skills. The qualities hiring managers trust are not tied to a country or a background. They can be built anywhere.

How do you become the candidate they hire?

Stop trying to be the smartest person in the room. Be the one they trust with cloud and AI infrastructure roles at two in the morning.

Get the free Cloud Project Portfolio Blueprint and build proof instead of another certificate.

Book your free career strategy call and get an honest read on how you would interview today.

The Apex Institute is an IT career training company that trains working professionals in cloud engineering, DevOps and AI infrastructure, helping them move into the roles employers are struggling to fill as AI adoption accelerates. Students have reported more than $11 million in job offers to date. Individual results vary and are not typical. Learn more at apexedu.io.

data.title: Canada announces retaliatory tariffs on U.S. goods after trade talks break down
data.description:
By Rey Mashayekhi

Canadian Prime Minister Mark Carney speaks at a press conference in Ottawa, Ontario, on Saturday after trade talks with the U.S. collapsed.

Canada Prime Minister Mark Carney on Saturday announced his country would impose "dollar-for-dollar" tariffs on U.S. goods - a retaliatory measure after trade talks between the two nations broke down late Friday, leading the U.S. to levy 50% tariffs on roughly $20 billion in Canadian goods.

Carney said the the tariffs would take effect next month on the Tuesday after Labor Day, and would focus on sectors including steel, dairy, paper, electronics, appliances and agricultural equipment.

"While we believed earlier this week that we were moving toward a mutually beneficial [trade] agreement, in recent days, the U.S. proposed new terms that were uneconomic, unfair and undermined the net benefits to Canada, calling into question the reliability of any deal," Carney said at a press conference in Ottawa.

"In short, they asked too much and offered too little," the prime minister added.

The two sides entered trade negotiations after President Donald Trump announced 50% tariffs on Canadian goods last month - the latest in a series of trade disputes between the North American neighbors since Trump returned to the White House last year. The U.S. president has taken a similar stance against American trade partners globally.

After promising that the duties would go into effect on Wednesday, Trump back down on that threat late Tuesday, saying that the U.S. and Canada were close to a deal. Yet talks collapsed on Friday evening, and the U.S.'s 50% tariffs on Canadian imports took effect shortly after midnight Saturday.

This is a developing story and will be updated.

-Rey Mashayekhi
